concepts.title: First Law — Inertia
concepts.contentHtml:
An object at rest stays at rest, and an object in motion stays in motion at constant velocity, unless acted on by a net external force.

Things don't naturally slow down — friction does. In space, a thrown ball would coast forever.

This was Galileo's revolutionary insight: motion needs no cause; only changes in motion do. It overturned 2000 years of Aristotelian physics that said objects 'wanted' to come to rest.

concepts.title: Second Law — F = ma
concepts.contentHtml:
The net force on an object equals its mass times its acceleration.

This means a heavier object needs more force to accelerate the same amount, and the same force produces less acceleration on heavier objects. Push a shopping cart — easy. Push a car — much harder.

Force is measured in newtons (N). One newton accelerates a 1 kg mass at 1 m/s².

F = ma is arguably the most consequential equation in human history — it sent us to the moon.

concepts.title: Third Law — Action and Reaction
concepts.contentHtml:
For every action, there is an equal and opposite reaction.

When you push on a wall, the wall pushes back on you with the same force. When a rocket pushes hot gas downward, the gas pushes the rocket upward — that's how rockets work in vacuum.

The two forces always act on different objects. That's why they don't cancel. The force you exert on the wall and the wall on you are paired but separate.

title: Energy & Momentum
description: Two quantities that nature jealously conserves

concepts.title: Kinetic and Potential Energy
concepts.contentHtml:
Kinetic energy is energy of motion: KE = ½mv². Doubling speed quadruples kinetic energy — that's why car crashes get exponentially more dangerous.

Potential energy is stored energy waiting to be released. Gravitational potential energy: PE = mgh (mass × gravity × height). Lift a book higher and it has more potential energy — drop it and that becomes kinetic.

Energy is measured in joules (J). One joule lifts a small apple about one meter.

concepts.title: Conservation of Energy
concepts.contentHtml:
In a closed system, total energy is conserved — it cannot be created or destroyed, only transformed.

A pendulum swings: at the top it's all potential energy (briefly motionless), at the bottom all kinetic (fastest). Sum stays constant.

In the real world, friction converts some energy to heat. The total still sums to the same — heat just isn't useful for mechanical work.

This principle, called the First Law of Thermodynamics, is one of the most ironclad laws in physics.

concepts.title: Momentum
concepts.contentHtml:
Momentum is mass × velocity: p = mv. It's a vector — direction matters.

Like energy, momentum is conserved in a closed system. When two billiard balls collide, the total momentum before equals the total momentum after.

This is why guns recoil: the bullet's forward momentum equals the gun's backward momentum (the bullet is much faster because it's much lighter).

Conservation of momentum lets us predict collisions without knowing the messy details of the forces involved.

title: Forces & Friction
description: All the pushes and pulls — and why surfaces resist sliding

concepts.title: Types of Forces
concepts.contentHtml:
Forces come in several common varieties:

— Gravitational: every mass pulls every other mass. On Earth's surface, simplifies to weight (W = mg).
— Normal: a surface pushing back perpendicular to itself. The floor holds you up.
— Tension: a pulling force transmitted through a rope, string, or cable.
— Applied: any direct push or pull you exert.
— Friction: opposes sliding between surfaces.

The net force is the vector sum of all forces — that's what drives F = ma.

concepts.title: Static vs Kinetic Friction
concepts.contentHtml:
Friction comes in two flavors:

Static friction prevents motion that hasn't started yet. It adjusts to match whatever sideways force is applied — up to a maximum.

Kinetic friction acts on already-moving objects. It's typically a bit weaker than the maximum static friction, which is why it's harder to start pushing a heavy box than to keep it sliding.

Both depend on the normal force and a coefficient of friction (μ) that captures how rough/sticky the surfaces are.

concepts.title: Free Body Diagrams
concepts.contentHtml:
A free body diagram isolates one object and draws every force acting on it as an arrow.

For a book on a table: gravity pulls down, normal force pushes up. Sum to zero — book stays put.

Push the book sideways: applied force right, friction left, gravity down, normal up. If applied beats friction, net force right; book accelerates.

Free body diagrams are the single most useful tool in mechanics. Drawing one before doing math saves more errors than any other habit.

title: Circular & Rotational Motion
description: Spinning, orbiting, and the physics of going in circles

concepts.title: Centripetal Force
concepts.contentHtml:
An object moving in a circle is constantly changing direction — that's acceleration, even at constant speed.

This centripetal acceleration always points toward the center of the circle. The force causing it is the centripetal force: F = mv²/r.

For a car turning, friction provides it. For Earth orbiting the Sun, gravity provides it. For a ball on a string, tension provides it.

Without centripetal force, objects fly off in a straight line — Newton's First Law in action.

concepts.title: Angular Velocity and Torque
concepts.contentHtml:
Rotational motion has its own vocabulary. Angular velocity (ω) is how fast something rotates — radians per second.

Torque (τ) is the rotational analog of force: τ = r × F. It depends on how hard you push AND how far from the pivot you push.

This is why door handles are placed far from the hinge — same effort, more torque.

Torque is what changes rotational motion, just as force changes linear motion.

concepts.title: Moment of Inertia
concepts.contentHtml:
Moment of inertia (I) is the rotational analog of mass — it measures how hard it is to start or stop a rotation.

Unlike mass, I depends on how the mass is distributed. Mass far from the rotation axis contributes more.

This is why an ice skater spinning with arms out spins slowly; pulling arms in (mass closer to axis) makes them spin faster — angular momentum is conserved.

The rotational version of F = ma is τ = Iα (torque equals moment of inertia times angular acceleration).

title: Gravity & Orbits
description: From falling apples to planetary orbits

concepts.title: Newton's Law of Universal Gravitation
concepts.contentHtml:
Newton's revolutionary insight: the same force that pulls an apple to the ground holds the Moon in orbit.

Every mass attracts every other mass with a force:

F = GMm/r²

where G is the gravitational constant, M and m are the two masses, and r is the distance between them.

The force weakens with the square of distance. Double the distance = quarter the force. This 'inverse-square law' shows up everywhere in physics — it follows naturally from forces spreading over expanding spheres.

concepts.title: Orbits — Falling Around
concepts.contentHtml:
An orbit is just falling sideways fast enough to miss the ground.

The Moon is constantly being pulled toward Earth — but it's also moving sideways at ~1 km/s. By the time gravity has pulled it 'down' a bit, it's traveled sideways enough that the curved Earth has fallen away beneath it. Net result: it never gets closer.

Orbital speed depends on altitude: higher orbits are slower. The ISS orbits at ~7.7 km/s; geostationary satellites at ~3.1 km/s.

concepts.title: Kepler's Laws
concepts.contentHtml:
Before Newton, Kepler discovered three empirical laws of planetary motion (1609–1619):

1. Orbits are ellipses, with the Sun at one focus — not perfect circles.
2. Equal areas in equal times — planets move faster when closer to the Sun.
3. T² ∝ r³ — orbital period squared is proportional to the cube of the average distance.

Newton later showed all three follow mathematically from his inverse-square law of gravity. Empirical observation predicted what theory would later explain — a beautiful example of how science progresses.

concepts.title: Independence of Horizontal and Vertical
concepts.contentHtml:
A projectile in flight (ignoring air resistance) moves independently in horizontal and vertical directions. Horizontal velocity stays constant; vertical velocity changes due to gravity.

Drop a ball and shoot a ball horizontally at the same instant — they hit the ground simultaneously. The horizontal motion doesn't affect the time to fall.

This decomposition turns a complicated 2D problem into two independent 1D problems — one of physics' great simplifications.

concepts.title: Range and Maximum Height
concepts.contentHtml:
For a projectile launched at angle θ with speed v₀ on level ground (no air resistance):

Range: R = v₀² sin(2θ) / g — maximized at θ = 45°.
Max height: H = v₀² sin²θ / (2g) — maximized at θ = 90° (straight up).

Real artillery and ballistics deviate from these simple formulas because of air resistance, which depends on velocity nonlinearly. Optimal launch angle is reduced to about 30-35° for typical projectiles.

concepts.title: Trajectory in Real Air
concepts.contentHtml:
Air drag scales roughly as v² for fast objects (baseballs, missiles) and as v for slow ones (spores, falling rain at low speed).

Drag breaks the symmetry of the trajectory: the descending part is steeper than the ascending. A baseball reaches maximum range at about 35°, not 45°.

Ballistics, golf, basketball, and military targeting all live with air resistance. Computers solve the equations of motion numerically — closed-form solutions exist only for clean idealizations.

title: Center of Mass & Stability
description: Why some things tip over and others don't

concepts.title: What Is Center of Mass?
concepts.contentHtml:
The center of mass of an extended object is the weighted-average position of all its mass elements.

For external forces, an extended body behaves as if all its mass were concentrated at the center of mass. A wrench thrown spinning across a table — chaotic looking — has a center of mass that travels in a clean parabola.

For a uniform symmetric object, the center of mass is at the geometric center. For irregular shapes, you can find it by hanging it from two different points and finding the intersection of the plumb lines.

concepts.title: Stability Conditions
concepts.contentHtml:
An object is stable if a small displacement raises its center of mass — gravity will pull it back. Unstable if a displacement lowers the CM. Neutral if neither.

A pyramid sitting on its base: stable. The same pyramid balanced on its tip: unstable. A ball on a flat table: neutral.

For practical stability, the line from the center of mass to the ground must fall within the base of support. Wider base = more stable. That's why race cars are wide and low.

concepts.title: Toppling vs Sliding
concepts.contentHtml:
Push horizontally on a tall, narrow object. As you increase the force, the object will either slide (if friction is low) or tip (if friction is high but the base is narrow).

Tipping condition: the line of action of the applied force, extended downward, falls outside the base of support — torque about the leading edge becomes destabilizing.

Tall ships, cranes, and humans rely on continuous balancing because their bases are small relative to their heights. Walking is a controlled forward fall caught by stepping.

title: Lagrangian & Hamiltonian Mechanics
description: A more powerful way to see classical motion

concepts.title: The Principle of Least Action
concepts.contentHtml:
Newton: F = ma, given the forces, integrate equations of motion forward.

Lagrange/Hamilton (1788+): every classical trajectory is the one that extremizes the action S = ∫L dt, where L = T − V is the Lagrangian (kinetic energy minus potential energy).

This single principle reproduces all of Newtonian mechanics — and naturally extends to fields, relativity, and quantum mechanics. It's a deeper way of seeing the same physics.

concepts.title: Generalized Coordinates
concepts.contentHtml:
A pendulum has only one degree of freedom (the angle θ), not three (x, y, z). Lagrangian mechanics lets you use whatever coordinates fit the problem — angles, distances along surfaces, anything.

The Euler-Lagrange equations give the equations of motion for any coordinate q:

d/dt(∂L/∂q̇) − ∂L/∂q = 0.

Constraints (a bead on a wire, a pendulum's fixed length) are automatically built into the choice of coordinates. No need to track constraint forces.

concepts.title: Symmetries and Conservation
concepts.contentHtml:
Noether's theorem (1915): every continuous symmetry of the Lagrangian gives a conserved quantity.

• Time-translation symmetry → energy conservation.
• Space-translation symmetry → momentum conservation.
• Rotation symmetry → angular momentum conservation.

This is one of the most beautiful results in all of physics. It explains why conservation laws exist and connects them directly to the symmetries of nature.
